lines.text: Karsa Station is dying slowly, the way a lit window dies when the building empties. The convoy leaves in nine hours.
Three of us clear the north spine. The Procession loads behind us. Nobody stops to count.
For the record, the Roll says we are two thousand. I count three of us.
The lock cycles. Behind them the station's lights go out one deck at a time.
Four hundred and six aboard. I will say it again tomorrow.
Say it as many times as it takes.
The Weir is where the fleet came to die: a field of hulls with their running lights still blinking.
Follow my lantern. Hulls on the left are cover. Hulls on the right are graves.
If it blinks, it has not finished dying. Do not trust it.
They find fuel, and a hull with seventeen names still painted on the bulkhead.
Seventeen. I will keep them.
Fuel for nine days. I counted twice.
Pellam Dock is a long iron mouth. The Procession needs eleven hours at its throat.
Hold the gantries. Let the tugs finish. Four on each side.
The muster drop is scheduled for midnight. I would rather it was not.
The first drop falls through the dock's cold air at midnight. It is not supplies.
Say his name. Say it before it stands.
Do not. It is not him.
The Orchard Ring grows food in the dark, under lamps older than the war.
Families in the lower gardens. The Hegemony is sweeping from the aft.
I know the paths. Let me show you.
Wren walks out with them, carrying a name that is not hers.
You are not enlisted.
Then count me as a guest.
The Quiet Wards is a hospital hulk drifting dark. Someone has left the lights on in the long ward.
There are eighty of them. They cannot be moved without us.
A polite voice is on the net. It says it only wants to talk.
Provost Orrick's first transmission comes in clean and courteous.
Captain. Stand down and be counted. The Procession will be resettled. No one will be hurt.
Say it to the wounded.
The Foundry ship Anselm hangs in the dark, still working. Inside, the vats are warm.
I can hear it from here. A hum under the teeth.
Everything we have lied about is in there.
Rows of bodies hang in the fluid, each with a slot number and no face.
That one has my brother's number.
We choose. Break the vats, or take the key.
Cinder Market runs on light and rumour. Everything is for sale, including the way out.
We trade. We do not linger. Anyone who lingers gets counted.
You do not know me. I know him.
Oriel Vance sits among them with a stolen ledger and a stillness the squad recognises.
I can tell you how he thinks. I cannot tell you why he does.
Why should we trust you?
The Mirror Gate opens for forty minutes in every day. The Hegemony holds its frame.
Forty minutes. Eleven ships. Do the arithmetic.
I can jam the net. Not for long.
The last ship slips through as the gate closes; its lights fold into the dark.
Eleven. Eleven. Eleven.
I think she says it so she does not have to say the others.
The Reliquary Lane is a memorial that drifted: ten thousand hulls, each one named.
Every hull has a roll. Read none of them. We have no time.
I will read one.
Two of Orrick's officers lie still in the half-light. Their replacements are already on the way.
Count them. He will.
Count them.
A hundred metres of hull, one door, and the whole Procession behind it.
I hold the door.
You hold it with us.
Orrick comes through the smoke alone, unhurried, courteous. His face has nothing in it.
He taught me the course. I never once saw him blink.
Captain, I have been trying to reach you. May I count you?
Tamsin's Rest is a relay station at the lip of the dark. Its archive still answers.
The Roll has a second copy here. It is not what we have been carrying.
Show me.
Two hundred and twelve thousand names, and fourteen companies that never existed.
I knew. I have known since Karsa. I am sorry.
My mother is on this list. Is she dead, or just counted?
Vesper Reach opens its dark door slowly. The Keepers stand in rows without weapons.
The Procession is welcome. The Roll is welcome. Weapons and tethers are not.
Then we are not.
At the threshold, the squad has to decide what it is.
I have six officers and no one to command. I would like, very much, to be counted.
Then count with us.

choices.text: Read the Roll at the door.

lines.text: A tug turns slowly end over end, its crew tapping on the hull.
Three of them. Still counting seconds.
Bring them in.
Someone has lit a beacon. In this dark, that is a confession.
It is a Hegemony frequency. They are already coming.
Put it out.
A picket sits across the lane, polite and patient.
They will ask for papers. Do not have any.
Gladly.
A dead cruiser, still warm, with a claim-jumper's flag already on it.
Everything in there is a reserve.
Be quick. Be quiet.
One convoy ship has stopped answering and begun to turn.
They are frightened. That is all it is.
Then we talk first.
A relay has gone silent in the middle of the lane.
Colourless. No hum at all. I do not like it.
For the record, silence is also a signal.
The last fuel tender limps beside the convoy, trailing frost.
Lose it and we walk.
Then we do not lose it.
A lamp-keepers' dock is going dark, one lantern at a time.
I know this place. Someone has to be there.
Go.
The squad forms up in the cold light. One slot on the roll is empty, and will not be for long.
We read the name. Or we do not.
The name is spoken once, slowly, into the quiet.
It is not much. It is what we have.
No one speaks. The recyclers hum. The slot waits.
That is also a way to grieve.
The muster drop opens. A body steps out wearing the dead soldier's number and nothing else.
There is the hum.
Present.
Captain. I am Provost Orrick of the Retrieval Bureau. Stand down and be counted. The Procession will be resettled, and no one will be harmed.
Captain. I regret the losses on both sides. My offer stands. Be counted, and you will be fed.
Captain. Two of mine are replaced. Two of yours are replaced. We are converging. Be counted.
Captain. The count is closer than it was. I find I do not mind it. Be counted.
Captain. Four replaced. The terms are unchanged. The terms are the terms.
Captain. Five. Be counted.
Count: six. Count: one. Terms: unchanged. Terms: unchanged. Be counted.
Teodor.
It was Teodor. I had forgotten that I was permitted to say so.
Night shift. The convoy ticks and settles.
Four hundred and six. Four hundred and six.
Go to sleep, Mara.
I name them after the ones we lose. That one is Dov.
Dov is not dead.
It is a good star. Keep it.
Two-forty. Breathe.
Who are you talking to?
Whoever is listening.
I have it.
You do not have to have everything.
Someone does.
Listen. Under the recyclers. Do you hear the hum?
No.
Good. Stay that way.
Three hundred and four. Shall I say them?
All of them?
Slowly.
I have lost this war once, kid.
And?
And I am still walking. That is the whole lesson.
I keep two ledgers. One for the rounds. One for the jokes.
Which is longer?
Do not make me count.
For the record, I have not slept since Karsa.
Neither have I.
That is not for the record.
The Procession passes the black glass and the door closes behind it, gently.
Read them all. From the first.
It takes eleven days. At the end, every hollow in the dark stops and stands. The lights stay on.
The squad holds the door. The muster drops keep coming, and the slots keep filling.
Forty years is a long time to count.
Every year there are fewer people and more of them standing still. Someone, somewhere, keeps the lantern lit.
The squad is counted, and found to be exactly what the ledger said.
Thank you, Captain. The Procession will be resettled.
It is safe. It is ordinary. No one remembers the lanterns.
Orrick sits in a room of six silent bodies and does not speak.
Count with us.
One.
It is the first number he has not asked anyone else to be.
